A T-learner fits one model per treatment arm and takes uplift as the difference of the two predictions, P(treatment) - P(control).
The models are ranked by AUUC (area under the uplift curve), the Qini coefficient, and uplift at top-k: if you act on the top 20 percent scored by uplift, how much extra response do you get.
N-day retention is the share of a signup cohort that is active exactly N days after signup; D1, D7, and D30 are the standard checkpoints.
Rolling retention is fairer for products with sporadic usage: it asks whether a user was active at least once in a window, such as days 7 to 37, rather than on one exact day.

For each step you count the distinct sessions that reached it, then compute step-to-step conversion (this step divided by the previous) and overall conversion (this step divided by the first).
Cohort LTV must be compared at the same age: a cohort that signed up last month looks smaller than one from six months ago simply because it has had less time to spend, not because it is worse.
The gap between first-touch and lifetime revenue is itself a signal: large gaps mark channels with repeat-purchase potential worth investing in.
The matrix is triangular: a cohort that signed up last month has only one column observed, while an older cohort has many.
Stickiness is DAU divided by MAU: it measures how often, within a month, the average active user is active.
A running total uses SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING).

The gaps-and-islands pattern labels consecutive runs by subtracting a row number from the date: day minus row_number is constant within one consecutive run and jumps at a gap, turning runs into groupable keys.
